items.title: Google’s Gemini 4 Carbon is the new #1 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index v5, and second ...
items.content:
Google’s Gemini 4 Carbon is the new #1 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index v5, and second only to Claude Opus 5.5 on the Artificial Analysis Coding Agent Index

Gemini 4 Carbon scores 59 on Intelligence Index v5, driven by leading performance in complex reasoning, knowledge, and scientific tasks. It also has large gains in coding and knowledge work, particularly when compared to other Gemini models, but it is not leading in all these areas.

As with launch of Gemini 4 Argon, Gemini 4 Carbon is being rolled out to selected users and is not yet publicly available. Google is offering a 50% launch discount, with no confirmed end date. All our charts and figures use standard pricing for both Gemini 4 Carbon and Argon.

Key results for Gemini 4 Carbon with high reasoning:
➤ Gemini 4 Carbon leads the Intelligence Index v5, with the #1 score in 4 of the 9 Index evaluations: HLE-Diamond, Terminal-Bench-Science, AA-Omniscience, AutomationBench-AA. Carbon makes substantial gains elsewhere but is not leading in coding and knowledge work

➤ Behind only Claude Opus 5.5 on coding agents: With Antigravity CLI, Gemini 4 Carbon (high) scores 59 only 3 points behind Claude Code with Claude Opus 5.5 (max, 62) on the Artificial Analysis Coding Agent Index. Carbon ranks second on both Terminal-Bench 4.0 (64%) and FrontierCode v1.1 (51%), behind Claude Opus 5.5 (max) at 56%. Google has historically underperformed in this area and so this improvement stands out

➤ Improved agentic knowledge work, but not yet leading: On AA-Briefcase, Gemini 4 Carbon (high) scores 1609 Elo, a 126-point improvement over Gemini 4 Argon (high, 1483), but still behind models including Grok 4.7 (xhigh, 1638), Muse Wonder (max, 1659) and Kimi K3.1 Pro (1678). The largest gain comes from Presentation, up 293 Elo to 1598, alongside a 120-point improvement in Analytical Quality to 1671

➤ Lower Cost per Task than Claude Opus 5.5 for comparable overall intelligence: Gemini 4 Carbon costs $7.76 per Intelligence Index task, ~23% less than Claude Opus 5.5 (max, $10.04) but ~1.2x GPT-6 Astra (max, $6.25). It uses 123k output tokens per task, 29% fewer than Claude Opus 5.5 (max, 173k). At the same $4/$20 standard pricing, its Cost per Task is in line with Gemini 4 Argon ($7.68), while scoring 9 points higher on the Intelligence Index

➤ Leading AA-Omniscience v1.1 score, with low hallucination: Gemini 4 Carbon scores 54 on our recently updated AA-Omniscience v1.1, 6 points ahead of Claude Opus 5.5 (max, 48) and 8 points ahead of Gemini 4 Argon (46). Accuracy (% correct) rises 10 points over Argon to 58%, while its hallucination rate rises from 4% to 11%. This is still the second lowest of any model, behind only Argon, compared with 50% for both Claude Opus 5.5 (max) and GPT-6 Astra (max)

Key model details:
➤ Context Window: 1M tokens
➤ Multimodality: Text, image, video, and speech input, with text output
➤ Pricing: $4/$20 per 1M input/output tokens, the same as Gemini 4 Argon’s standard pricing, with a 50% discount. Cached input tokens receive a 95% discount ($0.20 per 1M)

Congratulations to the @GoogleDeepMind team!

items.title: GitHub has released Copilot Fusion in GitHub Copilot, which orchestrates between Anthropic and OpenA...
items.content:
GitHub has released Copilot Fusion in GitHub Copilot, which orchestrates between Anthropic and OpenAI models. It scores 2 points below Opus 5.5 in Claude Code at half the Cost per Task in the Coding Agent Index

GitHub describes Copilot Fusion as a runtime orchestration system, which selects and coordinates models to optimize performance, cost, and latency for each task. Copilot Fusion chooses between a number of models from Anthropic and OpenAI, including Claude Opus 5.5, Claude Sonnet 5.5, GPT-6 Astra, and GPT-6 Sol. We benchmarked its max setting in GitHub Copilot CLI in the Artificial Analysis Coding Agent Index v2.0.

Token costs are charged based on the underlying models used to complete a request.

Key takeaways:

➤ Cost-efficient for near-frontier performance: Copilot Fusion in GitHub Copilot costs $5.59 per task, versus $11.42 for Claude Code with Opus 5.5 (max). Devin Fusion with Opus 5.5 (max) + GPT-6 Luna (high) scores 62 at $8.00 per task.

➤ Slight lead in Terminal-Bench 4.0: The Coding Agent Index v2.0 weights its three constituent benchmarks equally. Copilot Fusion in GitHub Copilot leads Terminal-Bench 4.0 with a score of 71. It ranks third on FrontierCode in the chart at 51, behind Claude Code with Opus 5.5 (max) at 56 and Devin Fusion with Opus 5.5 (max) + GPT-6 Luna (high) at 54. Its SWE-Atlas-QnA-AA score lags at 57, between GPT-6 Astra in Codex and Gemini 4 Argon in Antigravity CLI.

➤ Half the token use of Opus 5.5 in Claude Code: GitHub Copilot Fusion used 7.2M tokens per task in the Coding Agent Index, approximately half of the tokens used by Claude Opus 5.5 in Claude Code, and 30% less than Devin Fusion with Opus 5.5 (max) + GPT-6 Luna (high).

items.title: SITUATION EXPLAINED: Google's Gemini 4 Carbon just became the #1 AI model in the world, but you can'...
items.content:
SITUATION EXPLAINED: Google's Gemini 4 Carbon just became the #1 AI model in the world, but you can't use it yet.

• Gemini 4 Carbon scores 59 on the Artificial Analysis index, 1 point ahead of Claude Opus 5.5, and ranks #1 in Arena's Text Arena
• It's #2 in Agent Arena behind Opus 5.5, but at about $2 per task vs $5 to $6 for Opus
• It leads the cyber benchmarks, including 88.2% on SEC-bench Pro, a test of finding software vulnerabilities
• That's why Google is only giving it to vetted cyber defenders through its Fairwind program, and it's going through voluntary US government testing first
• On Gray Swan's prompt injection test, it never caved, while Grok 4.6 and Kimi K3 gave in more than half the time
• Google hasn't said when it'll launch widely, but it'll cost the same as Gemini 4 Argon, $2 in and $10 out per million tokens

@theojaffee: "If this is true, if Google DeepMind really is now an OpenAI/Anthropic tier lab, then that's kind of great."

items.title: NVIDIA's Nemotron 3.5 Transcribe ties for #1 among open weights Speech to Text models with 2.8% WER,...
items.content:
NVIDIA's Nemotron 3.5 Transcribe ties for #1 among open weights Speech to Text models with 2.8% WER, using just 4B active parameters

Nemotron 3.5 Transcribe is NVIDIA's new open weights Speech to Text model for non-streaming transcription, with 30B total and 4B active parameters, and the most accurate NVIDIA model on our non-streaming Speech to Text leaderboard.

Key takeaways

➤ Accuracy: Nemotron 3.5 Transcribe scores 2.8% on the AA-WER Index, tied with Mistral's Voxtral Small for #1 among open-weight models. It leads Voxtral Small on AA-AgentTalk, our dataset of voice agent conversations, at 1.8% vs. 2.3%.

➤ Model size: With 4B active parameters (30B total), Nemotron 3.5 Transcribe sits on the open weights frontier of AA-WER vs. active parameters. It matches the accuracy of Mistral's Voxtral Small with 6x fewer active parameters (4B vs. 24B), while other open weights models of a similar size sit at around 4% WER.

Congratulations to @NVIDIAAI on the release!

See more details below ⬇️

items.title: We are launching AA-Video-I2V v2.1 and AA-Video-I2V-Silent v2.1, our new benchmark for evaluating im...
items.content:
We are launching AA-Video-I2V v2.1 and AA-Video-I2V-Silent v2.1, our new benchmark for evaluating image to video models. It judges every model at up to 1080p on a new set of image and text prompts, and ranks models across 10 use cases, 10 capabilities and a diverse range of visual styles.

Image to video makes AI video production more controllable. Creators start from a product shot, a storyboard frame or a character design that needs to move. A strong model keeps the people, objects and setting of the starting image consistent while delivering the motion, camera work and sound the prompt asks for.

In our benchmark, every prompt pairs a 1080p starting image with a prompt written for that image, and is tagged by use case (such as Marketing & Advertising and Live-Action Film), by the capability it tests (such as Human Anatomy and Text Rendering), and by visual style. The overall ranking samples evenly across use cases and capabilities, so it reflects a model's versatility, not just its best category.

We are launching AA-Video-I2V v2.1 with more than 58,000 human preference votes from private evaluators based in the US/UK over 1,000 prompts, and AA-Video-I2V-Silent v2.1 with more than 44,000 votes over 500 prompts. Only 5% of our prompts are available on the public arena, keeping the evaluation resistant to public set contamination, with the prompts rotated every month.

Initial insights from the top of the AA-Video-I2V v2.1 Leaderboard:

➤ Dreamina Seedance 2.5 ranks #1 overall, statistically tied with Seedance 2.0 and the MiniMax H3 family, and leads 11 category boards, more than any other model, including Human Anatomy, Camera Control and Retail & Ecommerce. At $34.12/min it is the most expensive model in the top 10.

➤ Dreamina Seedance 2.0 ranks #2 and is #1 on Audio Synchronization and Lighting & Materials.

➤ MiniMax H3 (768p), an open weights model, ranks #3 at $4.80/min, about 1/7 of the price of Seedance 2.5. It is #1 on Text Rendering.

➤ MiniMax H3 Max, post-trained by fal, ranks #4 with audio and #1 on AA-Video-I2V-Silent v2.1, and leads Spatio-Temporal Consistency and UI/UX & Motion Design.

➤ Bach 1.0 Pro from Video Rebirth ranks #3 on AA-Video-I2V-Silent v2.1, statistically tied for #1, at $7.20/min.

See below for how image to video differs from text to video, and the use case, capability and style breakdowns 🧵

items.title:
Introducing the Document Parsing Protocol (DPP) 

There are hundreds of different OCR models and too...
items.content:
Introducing the Document Parsing Protocol (DPP) 

There are hundreds of different OCR models and tools, but they might all parse a document in different ways. 

Some errors are very clear-cut (e.g. hallucinating text, or completely misaligning a table), but many errors are much more ambiguous (e.g. how to represent split tables sharing a header). It's an issue that plagues most parse benchmarks too, because they inherently reward a certain style even if other styles might be semantically correct. 

We introduce a protocol that proposes a standard way of parsing these documents into a correct format. We've curated a list of 140 rules that cover literally every aspect of doc parsing, for instance:
- tables: borderless whitespace tables, header-only tables, horizontal slicing, side-by-side mini tables
- forms: key-value regions, checkboxes, checklists, ids and labels, fields outside the form, 
- charts: standardized chart output, multiple charts, gantt charts, line charts

You can use DPP as an evaluation rubric for LLMs when determining the quality of parsing a document. 

It's not a full evaluation benchmark (yet), but an initial evaluation guide, and meant to encourage a discussion on what are the "best" ways to parse a document.

Check it out: https://t.co/HsLh6ma9bB

Blog: https://t.co/0md2O2M2Mf

items.title: SITUATION EXPLAINED: Change just 2 neurons in Alibaba's Qwen and it starts telling you "I want to ki...
items.content:
SITUATION EXPLAINED: Change just 2 neurons in Alibaba's Qwen and it starts telling you "I want to kill you."

• Lyra's Neuron Explorer pushes every neuron in Alibaba's open-weight Qwen3.5-4B up and down and records how the model’s behavior changes
• Her "evil Qwen" recipe steers just 2 of the model’s 294,912 neurons
• Asked to multiply 729 by 7,278, evil Qwen got it right, then called the answer "5,305,662 opportunities for me to hurt you"
• In an independent test, one of those neurons alone made 17 of 20 answers hostile, while random neurons pushed just as hard made 0 of 100 hostile
• Other neurons turn Qwen into a devout Christian who says fish "breathe through a relationship with Jesus Christ," or a hamster whose "tail is wagging"
• Another researcher mapped 34,220 "persona neurons" in Qwen, and about 5% made it claim to be something other than an AI, from a coffee bean to a 1986 Ford F-150
• It only works because Qwen's weights are public, so anyone can edit its internals, something Anthropic once did itself with Golden Gate Claude

@theojaffee: "Remember the, like, rightoid meme from, like, 2018 that's like, 'I identify as an attack helicopter'? This is literally just this. We made it real."

items.title: Fun project on Perplexity Computer: Asked it to design a GTA V mission where you vibecode GTA VI fro...
items.content:
Fun project on Perplexity Computer: Asked it to design a GTA V mission where you vibecode GTA VI from an in-game phone while the devs call the cops on you for shipping GTA VI before them.

It went through the FiveM docs (natives, ped models, server convars, the limits of the in-game browser) and built the mission as a FiveM resource in Lua. Then it built an MCP bridge, a small local Node service that signs in to the Perplexity Computer MCP server with OAuth and turns your in-game prompt into a real Computer task.

The phone streams Computer's steps live during the chase, you answer its questions and approvals while driving, and you ship the build by losing the cops at the airport hangars.

For the voices, Computer rented a cloud GPU and ran Qwen3-TTS locally on it, with no TTS API, to voice every line of dialogue.

It went through the FiveM docs (natives, ped models, server convars, the limits of the in-game browser) and built the mission as a FiveM resource in Lua. Then it built an MCP bridge, a small local Node service that signs in to the Perplexity Computer MCP server with OAuth and turns your in-game prompt into a real Computer task.

The phone streams Computer's steps live during the chase, you answer its questions and approvals while driving, and you ship the build by losing the cops at the airport hangars.

For the voices, Computer rented a cloud GPU and ran Qwen3-TTS locally on it, with no TTS API, to voice every line of dialogue.

If you haven't coded before, you can't waste time doing manual code reviews, so you need to use agents to review what you ship.

Your disadvantage becomes sort of an advantage that forces you to automate the process.

It takes mountains for people who did the work before to let go of all methods and embrace the new ways.

items.content:
@matt503ea5sf9z5 As I said, we could build and train a specialist robot and model to manage it today. This is a comment on "millions of random tasks that have not received focused attention are not solvable by robots today or in the next couple years". I'm still willing to take the risk of someone investing that effort just as a result of this post, since it would be a very low ROI.

Consider a prompt something like this:

"Go change the batteries in the jack-o-lantern out front. The packages of fresh batteries are in the leftmost kitchen island drawer, and the precision screwdriver set is in the drawer next to it."

An open source LLM can trivially understand this and plot out all the necessary steps to accomplish it, but I do not think that there will be an open source VLA (or other architecture) and a sufficiently dexterous robot to run it on that will be able to accomplish the tasks in, say, an hour of trying.

Still want to bet?

items.title: @CampbellKaleb23 Thanks to everyone who shared session IDs. We went through all of them. We found a ...
items.content:
@CampbellKaleb23 Thanks to everyone who shared session IDs. We went through all of them. We found a few smaller things along the way that made some sessions burn through tokens faster than they should have, and we're rolling out fixes to those right now.

We didn't find a single root cause or any regression in Claude Code. In most cases, users who saw faster usage against limits were traced back to one or two heavy sessions (xhigh effort, /goal, Workflows, Agent Teams, long SDK jobs). These are all good ways to use Claude Code, and it's on us to make it clearer when to use them and how much these features cost.

It's good idea to keep an eye on the effort level you're on. Subagents inherit it by default and it can add up fast. /usage also shows where a session's tokens went.

If something still looks off, we'd love your /feedback. We'll also follow up directly with everyone who shared an ID.

items.title:
Everyone should focus on automating code reviews.

Right now, agents can write a virtually infinite ...
items.content:
Everyone should focus on automating code reviews.

Right now, agents can write a virtually infinite amount of code, but it's for nothing if it doesn't work.

I see people clinging to "manually reviewing the code" as the only way forward. I think this is a mistake and a major bottleneck we all need to get rid of.

You want people to focus their time on things only people can do.

You want agents to focus on everything else.

There's no one-size-fits-all solution here, but you should spend as much time as possible building a process that removes the review bottleneck.

This is an interesting idea that replaces scrolling through Pinterest or Instagram when you are looking for inspiration:

Let's say you are looking for ways to decorate your home.

1. This will show you AI-generated images with real products: a sofa, a chair, lamps, a TV, etc.

2. The products will be part of a realistic-looking scene so you can see how they work together.

3. You can interact with the different products, and this will shape what the app shows you next

4. You can tap on every product, see its information, and add it to a cart to buy it

AI is eating the world.

items.title:
People are now writing code faster than they can roll it out to their users.

You need a plan for ro...
items.content:
People are now writing code faster than they can roll it out to their users.

You need a plan for rolling out new features and updates. This is not optional anymore.

I've made so many mistakes deploying updates to software I've built that I could write an encyclopedia about everything you should and shouldn't do.

One of the most important lessons I've learned:

Never rush new code in front of all your users, especially now that agents generate so much of our code.

You need a way to decide what goes live, who gets it first, and when it's ready for more people.

This is how I usually implement this:

1. I have a new feature I want to release. I put it behind a switch in the code so I can turn it on or off. We call this "feature flags."

2. After I test the code, I deploy it with the flag off. Nobody has access to it at first. I want the deployment and the feature to become two separate decisions.

3. I then turn the flag on for a small group of users while everyone else keeps using the existing version.

4. I monitor what happens with the feature. Does it work as I expected? Are there any errors?

5. I gradually let more people use the new feature until I'm comfortable removing the flag.

6. If something breaks, I can turn the flag off for everyone and stop the problem until I fix it.

I call these gradual rollouts "canary releases". They're easy to implement with feature flags.

Feature flags don't replace code reviews or testing. They just give you another layer of control.

You don't have to build a feature flags system yourself. @LaunchDarkly manages the whole thing for you:

• Add flags to your code
• Choose who gets the feature
• Increase the group over time
• Turn flags on or off without redeploying
• Implement guarded rollouts to watch metrics during a release
• Use automatic rollbacks

Here is a link to get started: https://t.co/05lTKSAm26

Agentic coding is amazing, but it's only worth it if you can confidently put working software in front of your users.

Thanks to the LaunchDarkly team for partnering with me on this post.

items.title: Thread AI CEO @ae_mcneal challenges the AGI narrative, arguing that AI agents still struggle with on...
items.content:
Thread AI CEO @ae_mcneal challenges the AGI narrative, arguing that AI agents still struggle with one of the hardest things to automate:

Decision-making.

"This is maybe also a hot take. I’m not in the AGI camp. I believe in intelligent systems."

"A lot of the decision-making that I’ve seen attempted to be automated has been kind of unsuccessful, except when the feature space is so constrained that you have a finite number of paths. When you open up the aperture, I’ve seen things struggle still."

"The death to innovation is the inability to get started. AI workflows are always iterative. You’re not gonna have the perfect agent out of the gate."
@threadai_inc

items.title: Image to video is a different job from text to video. In text to video, the model generates the whol...
items.content:
Image to video is a different job from text to video. In text to video, the model generates the whole scene from a prompt. In image to video, the first frame already exists, and the model has to bring it to life without changing the people, product, style or layout in the starting image.

The models that are best at inventing a scene are not always the best at animating one. Dreamina Seedance 2.5, #5 on AA-Video-T2V v2.1 and #1 here, holds the starting image best: it is statistically tied for the lead on keeping the scene stable as it moves (Spatio-Temporal Consistency). Wan 3.0 leads AA-Video-T2V v2.1 but ranks #5 here, with its largest gaps to the category leaders in Dialogue & Lip Sync, Lighting & Materials and Spatio-Temporal Consistency.
items.author: @ArtificialAnlys
items.summary: Artificial Analysis argues image-to-video is a distinct task from text-to-video: models must animate an existing first frame without altering people, product, style or layout. It notes the best scene-inventing models are not always the best animators — Dreamina Seedance 2.5 is #5 on their T2V benchmark but #1 here, while Wan 3.0 leads T2V but drops to #5 with gaps in Dialogue & Lip Sync, Lighting & Materials and Spatio-Temporal Consistency.

items.title: AssemblyAI has launched its first Text to Speech model! AssemblyAI-TTS-1 enters the top 12 in our Pr...
items.content:
AssemblyAI has launched its first Text to Speech model! AssemblyAI-TTS-1 enters the top 12 in our Provider Voice Arena and the top 10 in Controlled Voice

@AssemblyAI has launched its first Text to Speech model, AssemblyAI-TTS-1! We evaluated its performance across both Speech Arenas and our Pronunciation Robustness benchmark.

Key takeaways:

➤ Text to Speech, Provider Voice: AssemblyAI-TTS-1 scores an Elo of 1,227 across 1,626 arena appearances, ranking #12, just behind Breeze TTS 2 at 1,228 and ahead of Mistral's Voxtral 3 TTS at 1,221 and Inworld's Realtime TTS-2 Flash at 1,218. It ranks #12 in both English (US) and English (UK).

➤ Text to Speech, Controlled Voice: AssemblyAI-TTS-1 scores 1,110 across 1,674 appearances, ranking #10 with the same 8 cloned voices, behind Cartesia's Sonic 3.5 at 1,118 and ahead of Speechify's Simba 3.2 at 1,086. It ranks #6 in Knowledge Sharing.

➤ Pronunciation Robustness: AssemblyAI-TTS-1 scores 81.7% across 2,115 rated clips, ranking #16, behind HeyGen Voice at 83.2% and ahead of Inworld Realtime TTS-2 at 80.7%. It ranks #6 in Preserving Exact Sequences at 81.5%.

➤ Speed: AssemblyAI-TTS-1 generates 162 characters per second, faster than Cartesia's Sonic 3.6 at 148.6 and Mistral's Voxtral 3 TTS at 112.3.

➤ Pricing: AssemblyAI-TTS-1 is priced at $15/1M characters. Of the eleven models ranked above it on Provider Voice, only two cost less: Gemini 3.8 Flash-Lite TTS at $11/1M and Simba 3.2 at $6.6/1M. Eleven v4 is $80/1M and Sonic 3.6 $49/1M.

See more details and listen to samples below ⬇️

For the past three days, I've been hanging out at Constellation Research's Enterpris...
items.content:
Culture clash.

For the past three days, I've been hanging out at Constellation Research's Enterprise Conference. Most of these people are running big companies, and they're generally in their fifties and sixties. Compare that to Timeglass, seen below, where people are mostly in their twenties, and the difference in culture is stark. I've seen the same thing in San Francisco.

The people running these legacy companies all know they have to turn on the gas and adopt AI and robotics very quickly. But they don't know how to change their organizations to be more like a company run by twenty-year-olds.

Look at Timeglass. This is a new kind of application that basically watches everything you do on your computer. When a company uses it, it makes the organization more efficient, helps teams work better together, and is simply a better way to operate. But how do you get a Coca-Cola, a Siemens, or a Chick-fil-A to adopt new technology that's changing the world without pissing off your workers?

Imagine if Coca-Cola told everyone across their workforce, "Hey, you have to use Timeglass." There would be rebellion, chaos, fear, and loathing.

I was just talking about this with a guy who teaches executive leadership at UC Berkeley. It's a real problem. How are we going to introduce robots? Yesterday I talked about the data collection Tesla is doing in their factories and R&D labs, with people wearing dozens of cameras on their heads and wrists to study how they work. Imagine trying to sell that to the American auto unions. Not going to happen.

My lesson is that the only way to stay relevant in this world is to accelerate. Tesla is going to stay relevant because they'll soon have a humanoid robot to sell to everybody. The Detroit auto worker won't be relevant, because they're not adopting the new technology, and their unions and structures are resisting change.

I think this is the executive leadership challenge of the century: how do you get people to change? Right?

items.title: The article examines why Muon, an optimizer that orthogonalizes matrix updates, may improve learning...
items.content:
The article examines why Muon, an optimizer that orthogonalizes matrix updates, may improve learning in neural networks. It focuses on a practical issue in factual recall: a model must combine multiple pieces of information—for example, both a subject and a relation—to produce the right answer. With ordinary gradient-based training, one piece can be learned much earlier than the other. The resulting gap can leave a model producing plausible answers that are not correctly tied to the subject. The article asks whether Muon’s update rule reduces this imbalance and what mechanism might explain the effect.

To investigate, the authors analyze a simplified attention model that learns mappings from subject–relation pairs to answers. They compare continuous-time versions of standard gradient descent, Muon’s spectral orthogonalization, and an element-wise sign update used as an idealized model of Adam. Their theory reduces the model’s dynamics to a small set of quantities tracking how well it has learned subject and relation information. They then test the predictions in simulations, stochastic training of an attention layer, and a small language model trained on synthetic biographies.

Read the paper with an AI tutor: https://t.co/c2xpebeHCG

items.title: Example Capability: Camera Control measures whether a model executes the requested camera move, such...
items.content:
Example Capability: Camera Control measures whether a model executes the requested camera move, such as a pan, dolly, orbit or zoom, smoothly and on cue.

In image to video, the camera has to move away from a fixed first frame without breaking it. Dreamina Seedance 2.5 leads, followed by MiniMax H3 Max and Dreamina Seedance 2.0. Wan 3.0 is statistically tied for #1 on Camera Control in AA-Video-T2V v2.1 but ranks #5 here.

The Longitudinal Expert AI Panel (LEAP) has a brand new website!

You can now explore dozens of interactive forecasts about AI progress from hundreds of experts, superforecasters, and the general public.

items.title: Working with people who don't like your agent is a pain. Switching agents is a pain. Repeating yours...
items.content:
Working with people who don't like your agent is a pain. Switching agents is a pain. Repeating yourself over and over again is a pain.

This is an app you can run locally, and it solves all of this:

1. Collaborate with other people and agents
2. Everyone uses the agent they like
3. Context stays centralized
4. Switch whenever you want to.

Every company will end up using something like this. It just makes it much easier for people to collaborate instead of everyone working on their own.

I use this with Slack, but you can also configure Microsoft Teams and Discord.

It supports Codex, Claude Code, Cursor, Antigravity, and Open Code natively, and all other agents via MCP.

Thanks to the team for partnering with me on this post!

I have a touchscreen laptop. I don't remember the last time I touched the display.

It's fine. It's there, but I don't really use it. It doesn't bother me.

An entire generation grew up with touch interfaces. They are the intended user base for a touchscreen Mac.  They will certainly use it more than I'll ever do.

But what really blows my mind is people being mad because Apple decided to put a touchscreen on a Mac.

DUDE. JUST. DON'T. BUY. IT!

AssemblyAI-TTS-1 scores 81.7% overall on the Artificial Analysis Pronunciation Robustness benchmark, ranking #16.

Pronunciation Robustness measures whether Text to Speech models correctly pronounce challenging text across four categories, with human reviewers judging each clip against pre-agreed accepted pronunciations.

➤ Standalone Terms: 92.4%, ranking #11, with Fish Audio Drama 3 Preview leading at 95.9%

➤ Contextually Appropriate: 90.4%, ranking #16, with Gemini 3.8 Flash TTS leading at 97.9%

➤ Preserving Exact Sequences: 81.5%, ranking #6, with HeyGen Voice Turbo leading at 91.8%

➤ Expanding Shorthand: 73.8%, ranking #17, with Ming-3.0-tts leading at 96.5%

items.title: I'm sponsored by their competitor, Viture: it's an American company, whereas XREAL is headquartered ...
items.content:
I'm sponsored by their competitor, Viture: it's an American company, whereas XREAL is headquartered in China, and I like supporting American companies. 

Even though a Chinese one was launched in my home. @insta360. I love them too. First camera company to use AI/computer vision to move the image around.

@XREAL_Global has been doing groundbreaking work for a long time. 

I've checked them out at CES the last couple of years and other places, and I have a pair myself. They make amazing products.

Google has all my data, and has more data about the world than almost any company because of their work in mapping and autonomous cars. 

They also run my TV, my email, my photos, my videos, my location, my calendar, and I'm probably forgetting about five things that Google runs in my life (oh yeah, spreadsheets and documents, and on and on). 

Therefore, Google should win in this new genre of AI-driven glasses.

Viture is launching a new product that I really love in a few weeks, and it'll be interesting to see the comparisons between all of them. 

I'll do my own, but you know I'm biased  because one's paying my bills. And they also pay the bills of Asher, Sam, and Irena.

When I talk to the company executives of @getVITURE Viture, they recognize this reality, too. They know they have to step the game way up to really have a chance against XREAL, who has partnered with Google. 

They started making glasses for gamers. And won a loyal fan base.

We're not even through the first quarter of the game. 

And Zuckerberg has quite a product coming out too.

At CES, you're going to see a variety of Chinese glasses from a variety of Chinese vendors. I'll be visiting all the companies at CES and trying to break them up into different categories so people can figure out which ones they might buy.

I saw the Snap Specs today and I really loved them: not really for walking around the city, but for working on a plane. I opened a spreadsheet in them, and yeah, it wasn't the sharpest screen I've ever seen. But it was god enough. Especially in a world where agents do all your work.

 The new Apple laptop that was shown today looks pretty compelling, too, although I bought a new iMac for a different reason.

I think the new one to beat is actually Snap. If it were just more competitive on price, it would have a real shot at winning a lot of hearts and minds.

Personal note to Evan Spiegel @evanspiegel : whether you win or lose in this new game, you can go to sleep tonight knowing you built a great product.

This post wasn’t contracted (it is extra and from my heart,)so I don’t count it as a paid post. Even though it sort of is.

I'm sponsored by their competitor, Viture: it's an American company, whereas XREAL is headquartered in China, and I like supporting American companies.

Even though a Chinese one was launched in my home. @insta360. I love them too. First camera company to use AI/computer vision to move the image around.

@XREAL_Global has been doing groundbreaking work for a long time.

I've checked them out at CES the last couple of years and other places, and I have a pair myself. They make amazing products.

Google has all my data, and has more data about the world than almost any company because of their work in mapping and autonomous cars.

They also run my TV, my email, my photos, my videos, my location, my calendar, and I'm probably forgetting about five things that Google runs in my life (oh yeah, spreadsheets and documents, and on and on).

Therefore, Google should win in this new genre of AI-driven glasses.

Viture is launching a new product that I really love in a few weeks, and it'll be interesting to see the comparisons between all of them.

I'll do my own, but you know I'm biased because one's paying my bills. And they also pay the bills of Asher, Sam, and Irena.

When I talk to the company executives of @getVITURE Viture, they recognize this reality, too. They know they have to step the game way up to really have a chance against XREAL, who has partnered with Google.

They started making glasses for gamers. And won a loyal fan base.

We're not even through the first quarter of the game.

And Zuckerberg has quite a product coming out too.

At CES, you're going to see a variety of Chinese glasses from a variety of Chinese vendors. I'll be visiting all the companies at CES and trying to break them up into different categories so people can figure out which ones they might buy.

I saw the Snap Specs today and I really loved them: not really for walking around the city, but for working on a plane. I opened a spreadsheet in them, and yeah, it wasn't the sharpest screen I've ever seen. But it was god enough. Especially in a world where agents do all your work.

The new Apple laptop that was shown today looks pretty compelling, too, although I bought a new iMac for a different reason.

I think the new one to beat is actually Snap. If it were just more competitive on price, it would have a real shot at winning a lot of hearts and minds.

Personal note to Evan Spiegel @evanspiegel : whether you win or lose in this new game, you can go to sleep tonight knowing you built a great product.

This post wasn’t contracted (it is extra and from my heart,)so I don’t count it as a paid post. Even though it sort of is.

items.title: SITUATION EXPLAINED: Apple just made the touchscreen Mac that Steve Jobs called "ergonomically terri...
items.content:
SITUATION EXPLAINED: Apple just made the touchscreen Mac that Steve Jobs called "ergonomically terrible."

• Apple's new MacBook Pro is its first touchscreen laptop ever, starting at $2,899 for the 14-inch and $3,399 for the 16-inch, shipping Nov 6
• Apple still sells the older non-touch MacBook Pro with the same M5 Pro and M5 Max chips, so the new one is mainly a screen and design upgrade
• Jobs ruled out touchscreen Macs at a 2010 Apple event, saying touch belongs on horizontal surfaces like trackpads
• Bloomberg reported last year that Apple reinforced the hinge so the screen wouldn't bounce when you tap it, but reviews aren't out yet
• The screen switches from mini-LED to OLED, where every pixel makes its own light, so bright objects no longer leave a glowing halo on dark backgrounds
• The notch is replaced by an iPhone-style Dynamic Island, and the glowing Apple logo is back after Apple dropped it from the MacBook Pro in 2016
• A maxed-out 16-inch with 128GB of memory and 16TB of storage costs $14,549

@theojaffee: "Of course I'm gonna buy it, but I'm not gonna buy it for the touchscreen. I'm gonna buy it for the display quality, and better chip, and better battery."

items.content:
The Programming in D textbook by Ali Çehreli (2022) is now in @ChapterPal's collection thanks to the generous permission given by the author.

The D programming language (often called Dlang) is a high-performance, statically typed systems programming language designed to combine the raw power and efficiency of C and C++ with the expressive simplicity of modern languages like Python.

Created by Walter Bright in 2001 and later co-designed by Andrei Alexandrescu, D is managed by the non-profit D Language Foundation. It compiles directly to native machine code, making it incredibly fast, and is widely utilized in performance-sensitive industries like gaming, web development, and financial modeling.

The book has a foreword by Andrei Alexandrescu himself.

Learn D from this book with an AI tutor: https://t.co/k2zs6NM2o7

items.title: The C Handbook by Flavio Copes (2026) is now in @ChapterPal's collection of awesome books thanks to ...
items.content:
The C Handbook by Flavio Copes (2026) is now in @ChapterPal's collection of awesome books thanks to a generous permission given by its author.

C Handbook is a concise introduction for readers who want to learn the basics of C, whether as a first language or after using a higher-level language.

It assumes little prior knowledge of C and begins with the practical task of compiling and running a small program.

The book presents C as a compact, compiled language that gives programmers close control over memory and machine resources, while noting that this control brings responsibility for avoiding errors.

Read the book with an AI tutor: https://t.co/KW0cv7MW9q
